title: POC weekly sync - INT8/FP8 sensitivity & rollout gatekeepers
topics: Benchmark alignment between hosted and on-prem
summary: Weekly POC check-in to review quantization sensitivity results. Action items include extended tail tests on customer infra, additional eval slices for entity extraction prompts, and decide canary gate thresholds (p95 latency, QA accuracy delta). Security wants audit log confirmation before private run.

Schedule a 30-minute canary planning session w/ Maya + Ethan for rollout gates the week of 2026-07-27

Jordan Reyes (DataForge) - upload 3 production prompt templates and 200 sample conversations (anonymized) to the shared S3 location - due 2026-07-19

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-15 14:30 UTC
Length: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Sophie (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Riley (Redwood Support), Jordan (DataForge ML Eng), Maya (DataForge Infra), Carlos (Product), Priya (Security)

Summary (auto): Weekly sync for quant POC; reviewed INT8 and FP8 runbooks, perf deltas, quality regressions on long-contexts, and next steps for canary gating.

[00:00] Sophie (AE): All right good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call and we'll get into results.
[00:07] Jordan (DataForge): Hey, Jordan here.
[00:09] Maya (Infra): Maya on infra.
[00:11] Carlos (Product): Carlos.
[00:12] Priya (Security): Priya, security.
[00:13] Ethan (SE): Ethan from Redwood.
[00:15] Sophie: Awesome. Ethan you have the screen for the results?
[00:19] Ethan: Yep pulling up the spreadsheet. Sorry there was a small delay on the hosted runs overnight, some of the H100 instances were queued, so we have a couple of partial runs but the important slices are there.
[00:33] Jordan: partial is fine, as long as tails are represented.
[00:36] Ethan: Right. So quick TL;DR before we dive into charts: INT8 gave us consistent memory reduction and average throughput improvements of about 1.6x to 1.9x on the H100 profile we used. FP8 had slightly better memory footprint but we saw more variability in quality on long-context QA and few-shot summarization slices.
[01:00] Carlos: variability meaning accuracy drop or hallucinations?
[01:02] Ethan: Mostly small accuracy deltas on entity extraction and occasional truncation artifacts with long K V cache re-use. So not full hallucinations but lower exact match on some extraction tests — usually in the 1-3% range, occasionally 4-6% on a narrow slice.
[01:20] Priya: when you say "KV cache" is that the prefix cache? we need clarity for security, like what gets stored and for how long.
[01:27] Ethan: Yeah prefix KV cache. It's in-memory on the serving node, not persisted to disk for the hosted run. For private we can configure ephemeral lifecycles and SDS to scrub caches after session end. We'll document that.
[01:40] Maya: Good — we'll need that for our compliance checklist.
[01:45] Sophie: I'll put that in the action items. Back to numbers: Ethan, can you call out p50/p95 differences?
[01:51] Ethan: Sure. Baseline FP16 p50 was 47ms, p95 115ms for the typical 512-token completion profile you gave us. INT8 p50 dropped to 28-32ms depending on sequence length distribution, p95 dropped to ~72-85ms. FP8 p50 was in the 30-35ms ballpark, but p95 had wider spread — sometimes close to baseline 110-130ms on the long-tail tests. So INT8 gave the most predictable tail improvement.
[02:20] Jordan: Those p95s are promising for us — our SLA target is p95 < 120ms. But the accuracy delta matters more for our QA pipelines.
[02:28] Carlos: Can you quantify the accuracy delta again?
[02:31] Ethan: For INT8 overall QA exact-match delta was typically within 0-2% compared to FP16. For FP8 we saw 2-6% on the longest-context slices and 0-1% on short prompts. Notably the few-shot summarization slice had a consistent ~3% drop when using our 8-shot prompts with FP8, likely due to the kernel scaling on attention matrices.
[02:58] Maya: Are these reproducible on customer infra or just on Redwood-hosted?
[03:03] Ethan: The runs were on Redwood-hosted H100 and an A100 profile. We've validated kernel parity but there are still differences in CUDA driver versions and MIG partitioning which can shift timing. We recommend running an extended tail test on a replica of your infra — that's one of the next steps.
[03:22] Sophie: Jordan, would you be able to spin up a small H100 replica or do you want us to run the test in your private environment?
[03:29] Jordan: We can spin up a replica in the same VPC but need the infra playbook from Maya's side. Maya?
[03:33] Maya: I can do that but need a checklist from Redwood — what kernel versions, container images, and KMS requirements. Also confirm whether you need access to our KMS or you'll use Redwood's ephemeral keys.
[03:48] Ethan: We'll share a runbook with exact images and driver versions. For KMS we can support both models: Redwood-managed keys for hosted verification or customer-managed KMS for private runs; security will want the latter for production.
[03:59] Priya: We will require KMS and HSM integration for production; for the replica test we can provide a restricted key for the run. We'll also want to validate audit log generation.
[04:10] Sophie: Noted. Back to the sensitivity: we also ran a precision sweep where we tested mixing FP16 layers with INT8 attention to see if a hybrid approach helps.
[04:21] Ethan: Right. The hybrid (attention INT8, MLP FP16) gave you nearly the INT8 latency gains with slightly smaller quality degradation than full INT8 on the extraction slices — like INT8-ish p95 but EX match deltas closer to 1% instead of 2%. It's an interesting compromise.
[04:39] Jordan: Can you explain the deployment complexity of the hybrid? Is it something we can roll out without kernel-level recompilation?
[04:45] Ethan: It's mostly a runtime config in our serving layer: kernel selection at operator boundaries. In a few models we had to pick specific fused kernels to avoid precision mix-ups, but we didn't need to recompile the model weights. It's a runtime flag in the Redwood serving profile and we can expose it as an option in the rollout.
[05:02] Carlos: That's actually appealing if we can keep quality high and get latency. From a product perspective the less engineering lift, the better.
[05:09] Maya: On cost — do you have unit-cost estimates for INT8 vs FP16 vs FP8 on the Dedicated pool?
[05:15] Ethan: Yes, rough numbers: INT8 lowers token cost by ~28-35% due to higher throughput and memory packing. FP8 lowers cost ~35-45% but with the caveat of potential quality delta that might increase re-generation or post-filtering costs. We'll attach the cost-per-1M tokens sheet.
[05:33] Jordan: How about memory headroom for batch sizes? We need to run bigger batches during nightly indexing jobs.
[05:40] Ethan: On INT8 you can increase batch sizes ~1.7-2x before hitting memory saturation versus FP16, FP8 gives even more headroom. That translates directly to throughput for batch workloads. For latency-sensitive small batch online workloads, INT8 is the most consistent improvement.
[05:58] Sophie: Let's talk rollback / canary gates — what are you recommending?
[06:02] Ethan: We recommend a two-tier gate: 1) safety gate — checks for major classification/QA regressions. If any critical slices exceed a threshold (we suggest >3% negative delta on core NER/extraction tasks or any increase in hallucination flags) the canary fails. 2) perf gate — p95 must be below your SLA target by a margin (we suggest p95 < SLA * 0.9 during canary). If both pass, expand canary; if either fails, auto-fallback to baseline FP16 for that route.
[06:34] Carlos: auto-fallback per route is important; we have a couple of high-risk routes where accuracy is non-negotiable.
[06:40] Ethan: We can pin routes to variants and do per-route fallbacks. Redwood's routing layer supports that.
[06:46] Jordan: How noisy are the canary metrics? we don't want false positives during business hours spikiness.
[06:50] Ethan: We'll use statistical tests over sliding windows — 95% confidence intervals, and require values to be sustained for 15 minutes before failing. Also multiple eval slices help reduce noise.
[07:02] Priya: For audit/compliance we need traceability: which model variant served which request and why the fallback occurred.
[07:08] Riley (Support): That's part of the trace logs we can surface, token-level trace, model-variant, region, and fallback reason. We'll include sample log entries in the security packet.
[07:19] Sophie: Great. Any immediate blocker on your side, Jordan?
[07:22] Jordan: The quality team wants more examples of the failure cases — can you surface the top 20 worst-performing prompts for FP8?
[07:30] Ethan: We have a ranked list; I'll export top 20 worst delta prompts and put them in the shared folder. Note some of them are edge-cases with very long contexts and unusual punctuation.
[07:40] Jordan: Useful. Also could you include a few counterfactuals where hybrid kernels helped?
[07:44] Ethan: Yes. I'll mark which ones responded better to hybrid.
[07:48] Carlos: One quick question on model variants: if we pin a route to the hybrid, can we still autoscale the serving pool?
[07:55] Ethan: Yes — hybrid uses the same autoscaling signal. The runtime will pick appropriate kernels across the pool; only the config differs.
[08:02] Maya: On the private run, we need to ensure container images are allowed in our registry policy. Do you provide signed images?
[08:09] Ethan: We can provide SBOM and signed container images. We'll also support attestation for runtime integrity if you require it.
[08:18] Priya: We'll want to review the SBOM and a copy of the signed image before we allow it in the registry.
[08:23] Sophie: We'll send that by EOD tomorrow.
[08:26] Ethan: Quick note on the FP8 variability: we dug into attention scaling factors and found that for some of your prompts the quant range clipping has greater impact when there are long numeric tokens and tables. That's why extraction on tabular long-context is worse.
[08:41] Jordan: That's the edge-case we saw in production last week. Is there a mitigation besides switching to INT8?
[08:47] Ethan: Two mitigations: 1) hybrid (INT8 attention + FP16 MLP) improved the extraction on those tabular prompts; 2) prompt pre-processing to normalize numeric tokens and reduce extreme ranges also helps. We can add an ingestion preprocessor for the nightly indexing stage.
[09:02] Maya: Will preproc add latency? We can't hurt the online path.
[09:06] Ethan: The preproc can run asynchronously for batch jobs. For online, lightweight normalization is possible and adds sub-ms overhead. We'll provide examples.
[09:16] Sophie: Okay next item: cost modeling for Dedicated versus hosted. Ethan, you had a slide?
[09:20] Ethan: Yes, but very high level here. For Dedicated, committed capacity pricing reduces cost variance and you can lock in INT8 throughput profiles. For hosted, we can experiment faster but unit-cost is a bit higher. For teams with steady throughput and strict SLAs, Dedicated + hybrid kernels looks compelling.
[09:38] Carlos: Are there any legal/compliance differences if we run INT8 versus FP16 in private?
[09:42] Priya: From our standpoint, it's the same model family; quantization is an implementation detail. We care about data residency, key control, and auditability.
[09:52] Sophie: We'll make sure the security packet clarifies that.
[09:55] Maya: One more infra question — you'll need at least CUDA 12.1 and a driver patch that fixes a memory leak we saw with fused attention kernels, can you confirm?
[10:04] Ethan: We suggested CUDA 12.1+ and a specific driver; I'll include exact versions in the runbook and we'll check compatibility with your AMIs.
[10:11] Jordan: timeline check: after the extended tail runs, when do you expect a canary ready?
[10:16] Ethan: If tails look consistent, we can stage a canary the week of 2026-07-27. That gives you a week for infra setup and security signoff.
[10:24] Sophie: sounds good. We'll plan a short canary planning session the week of the 27th.
[10:29] Carlos: Anything else?
[10:30] Jordan: One small ask — can the benchmark sheet include per-token energy or cost proxies? Our finance folks like to see that.
[10:36] Ethan: We'll add cost-per-1M-tokens and an estimated GPU-hour equivalent column.
[10:40] Priya: And auditing hooks for model-variant IDs that are human-readable.
[10:45] Riley: We'll make variant IDs include the precision and date so they're easy to map.
[10:50] Sophie: Okay let's recap action items...
[10:53] Sophie: Ethan to run extended tail on H100 private replica by 7/22.
[10:57] Sophie: Jordan to upload the three prompt templates by 7/19.
[11:00] Sophie: Sophie to send security packet and SOC2 excerpt by 7/17.
[11:03] Sophie: Maya to provide infra access matrix and confirm KMS constraints by 7/20.
[11:08] Jordan: And we'll review the top-20 worst FP8 prompts and decide whether to drop FP8 for certain routes.
[11:14] Ethan: I'll export that list and mark hybrid-friendly cases.
[11:18] Carlos: Great, thanks everyone.
[11:20] Maya: thanks.
[11:22] Priya: bye.
[11:23] Sophie: we'll follow up with calendar invites for the planning session. Thanks all.

(end of meeting)
